Lesson 1 of 4, about 13 minutes

Network firewalls: configuration for wired and wireless environments

Slide 5Network firewalls: configuration for wired and wireless environments

Terms to learn in this lesson

Network firewall
A device or virtual machine placed between network segments that forwards or drops each packet according to an ordered rule set. It protects many hosts at once; a host firewall (Class 6) protects only the machine it runs on.
Interface
A network connection of the firewall to one segment (physical port or VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network)). Rules are attached to interfaces.
5-tuple
The five values that identify a connection: protocol, source address, source port, destination address, destination port.
Stateful inspection
Filtering that remembers allowed connections in a state table and passes their replies without reading the rules again.
State table
The list of connections the firewall currently tracks, each described by its 5-tuple, its TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) state and a timeout.
First match
Rules of an interface are read from the top; the first rule that matches decides, and the rest are not read.
Default deny
Anything that no rule explicitly allows is dropped. Also called implicit deny.
Block and reject
Block drops the packet silently. Reject drops it and answers with a TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) reset or an ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) unreachable message.
VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network)
A logical network separated inside a switch; frames carry an 802.1Q tag that tells the switch and the firewall which VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) they belong to.
SSID (Service Set Identifier)
The name of a wireless network. One access point can broadcast several SSIDs and map each one to a different VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network).

A network firewall is a filtering device placed on the boundary between network segments. For each packet it receives, it answers a single question: forward it to the next segment, or drop it. The answer comes from an ordered list of rules written by the administrator, and from the firewall's memory of the connections it has already allowed.

Slide 6What a network firewall examines

1.1 What the firewall examines

Every packet carries headers. The firewall reads the fields that identify a conversation, called the 5-tuple: the protocol (TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) or UDP (User Datagram Protocol), or ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) for control messages), the source IP (Internet Protocol) address, the source port, the destination IP (Internet Protocol) address and the destination port. A port number identifies a service on a host: 443 is HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure), 445 is SMB (Server Message Block) file sharing, 22 is SSH (Secure Shell), 53 is DNS (Domain Name System), 3389 is RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol). The firewall also knows the interface on which the packet arrived, and that is the first thing it uses: a rule written for the LAN (Local Area Network) interface is never evaluated for a packet that arrived on the WAN (Wide Area Network) interface.

Slide 7Network firewall and host firewall work together

A network firewall differs from the host firewalls you configured in Class 6 in scope, not in principle. Windows Defender Firewall or UFW protects one machine and sees only that machine's traffic. NM-FW01 sees every packet that moves between zones and applies one policy to all the hosts of a zone at the same time. The two layers are complementary: the network firewall controls which zones may talk, and the host firewall controls which services each machine exposes, even to its own zone.

Slide 8Stateless and stateful filtering

1.2 Stateless and stateful filtering

A stateless filter judges each packet in isolation. To let a workstation browse the web, it needs one rule for the request (workstation to server, port 443) and a second, broad rule for every reply (server port 443 to any high port of the workstation). That second rule is dangerous, because an attacker can craft packets that look like replies.

A stateful firewall, such as the pf engine inside both pfSense and OPNsense, keeps a state table. When a rule allows the first packet of a connection, the firewall records its 5-tuple. Every later packet that belongs to that connection, in either direction, is compared with the state table first and passes without any rule being read. For TCP (Transmission Control Protocol), the firewall follows the three-way handshake: the client sends SYN (Synchronize), the server answers SYN-ACK (Synchronize-Acknowledgment), and the client confirms with ACK (Acknowledgment). A SYN-ACK (Synchronize-Acknowledgment) that matches no state entry is not a reply to anything and is dropped. Each entry has a timeout, so abandoned connections are removed and the table does not grow without limit.

The practical consequence for your rule set is simple and important: you write rules only for the direction in which a connection is opened. The replies are handled by the state table.

Slide 9First match and default deny

1.3 How the rules are evaluated

On pfSense and OPNsense, the rules of an interface are read from top to bottom, and the first match decides. A rule matches when every field it specifies (protocol, source, destination, destination port) fits the packet. Once a rule matches, its action is applied and no lower rule is read. When no rule matches, the packet meets default deny: it is dropped. Figure 1 shows the complete procedure. Official references: https://docs.opnsense.org/manual/firewall.html and https://docs.netgate.com/pfsense/en/latest/firewall/index.html.

Slide 10Three actions: pass, block, reject

Three actions are available. Pass forwards the packet and creates a state entry. Block drops it silently; the sender waits and eventually reports a timeout. Reject drops it and answers with a TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) reset (RST) or an ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) "unreachable" message, so the sender fails immediately. On the Internet-facing interface, block is preferred, because it gives no information to a scanner. On internal interfaces, reject can shorten troubleshooting. Whatever the action, turn on logging for blocks you care about: a logged block is evidence that the rule works.

Table 2. Rule actions and what a connection test observes
ActionWhat the firewall doesWhat the testing machine seesTypical use
PassForwards the packet and records the connection in the state tableConnection succeeds (if a service listens)Every flow of the zoning table
BlockDrops the packet silentlyTimeout after the waiting period (for example 3 seconds with nc -w 3)WAN (Wide Area Network) interface; explicit denies you want to log
RejectDrops the packet and returns a TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) reset or an ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) unreachable messageImmediate "connection refused" or "unreachable"Internal interfaces, to fail fast
Default denyDrops what no rule matched (acts like block)TimeoutImplicit last rule of every interface

A "connection refused" can also come from a host that received the packet but has no service on that port. Only the firewall log tells you which case it is.

Slide 11Two installation defaults to fix today

Two defaults of a fresh installation matter for today's lab. First, both appliances create an anti-lockout rule on the LAN (Local Area Network) interface that keeps the web interface reachable from the whole LAN (Local Area Network). In Class 11 you restricted management to NM-LWS01; replace the anti-lockout rule only after your own management rule is in place and tested. Second, a fresh LAN (Local Area Network) interface usually carries a default rule that allows "LAN (Local Area Network) net to any". That rule contradicts your zoning table, because it lets every workstation reach every zone. It must be replaced by the specific rules of Lesson 2, not kept "just in case".

Slide 12Wired zones: a dedicated interface or a VLAN

1.4 Wired environments: one zone, one interface or one VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network)

In a wired network, a zone can be connected to the firewall in two ways. With a dedicated interface, one network card of the firewall is cabled to the switch of that zone. With a VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network), one physical link carries several zones, and each frame carries an 802.1Q tag with the VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) number. The switch port of an ordinary workstation is an access port: it belongs to one VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) and removes the tag before the frame reaches the computer. The link between the switch and the firewall is a trunk: it carries several VLANs, each still tagged. On the firewall, each VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) appears as its own interface, with its own rules. In a virtual laboratory, the same result is reached with separate virtual networks, one per zone.

Whichever method you use, the rule of the zoning design is the same: a machine is in a zone because of the interface or VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) it is connected to, and the firewall enforces the zone through the rules of that interface.

Slide 13Wireless: two decisions at two places

1.5 Wireless environments: two decisions, at two places

A wireless client never talks to the firewall by radio. It talks to an access point (AP), and the access point forwards its frames onto a VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network). NorthMaple's access point NM-AP01 broadcasts the staff SSID (Service Set Identifier) "NorthMaple-Staff" and maps it to VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) 10, the user zone. From the firewall's point of view, a laptop on the staff Wi-Fi arrives on the LAN (Local Area Network) interface exactly like a wired workstation, and it is filtered by the same rules (Figure 2, after Example 1).

This means that security for wireless is decided twice. The access point decides who may join the SSID (Service Set Identifier) and how the radio link is protected: WPA3-Enterprise (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3, Enterprise mode) authenticates each person with 802.1X through a RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) server, while WPA3-Personal (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3, Personal mode) uses a shared passphrase protected by SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) (Wi-Fi Alliance: https://www.wi-fi.org/discover-wi-fi/security). The firewall decides what the client may reach once it has joined. A strong passphrase does not replace firewall rules, and firewall rules do not protect a radio link that anyone can join.

Slide 14Guest Wi-Fi and egress filtering

Because radio signals cross walls, visitors and personal devices must never land in the staff zone. The standard design, which you will add at Class 13, is a separate guest SSID (Service Set Identifier) mapped to its own VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) and its own GUEST interface, with three properties: rules that allow the Internet and nothing private, client isolation on the access point so that guest devices cannot reach each other, and, where it is useful, a captive portal on the firewall that shows the terms of use before access is granted. Finally, the access point is itself a network device: its management interface belongs in the device registry and must be reachable only from NM-LWS01, like the firewall's.

1.6 Filtering in both directions

Beginners often think of a firewall as a filter for incoming traffic only. Filtering the traffic that leaves a zone, called egress filtering, is just as important. If the user zone may only send HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) to the Internet and DNS (Domain Name System) to the firewall's own resolver, malware on a workstation cannot use an arbitrary port to contact its operator, and nobody can bypass the company resolver with an outside DNS (Domain Name System) server. Egress rules are written exactly like any other rule: on the interface where the traffic enters the firewall, which for outgoing traffic is the interface of the internal zone.

Slide 16Example 1: ten packets at NM-FW01 on a Monday morning

Real-life example, Lesson 1

Ten packets at NM-FW01 on a Monday morning

Task of this example

Predict, then verify, the decision NM-FW01 takes for ten packets that come from a wired workstation, a staff laptop on the corporate Wi-Fi, the Internet, the DMZ (Demilitarized Zone) and a visitor phone on the future guest SSID (Service Set Identifier).

How it relates to this lesson

The example applies every mechanism of this lesson in one run: the arrival interface, the state table, first-match evaluation, default deny, and the fact that a Wi-Fi client on the staff SSID (Service Set Identifier) is filtered by the LAN (Local Area Network) rules like a wired PC (Personal Computer).

Where this example and its deliverable return in the scheduled labs

  • LAB_05 part 2 (today): the same reasoning explains every allowed/blocked test you record in Chapter 5.
  • Class 13: the guest rows (P8, P9) become real when you add the guest Wi-Fi zone and its GUEST interface.
  • Final Project Chapter 7: rows 1, 3 and 4 of the resilience assessment use this logic (malware on a workstation, compromised DMZ (Demilitarized Zone) server, worm spreading).

It is 8:40 at NorthMaple. Nadia, an accountant, opens a tax website from the wired PC (Personal Computer) NM-WS01. Marc joins the staff Wi-Fi with his laptop NM-LT01 and opens the client-records share; out of curiosity he also types the firewall's address into his browser. The IT (Information Technology) administrator connects to the firewall over SSH (Secure Shell) from NM-LWS01. On the Internet, one host scans the office for Remote Desktop while a real visitor opens the public website. In the waiting room, a visitor's phone would join the guest SSID (Service Set Identifier) once it exists. At the same moment, the web server NM-WEB01, which you must assume could be compromised one day, tries to open SMB (Server Message Block) on a workstation.

  1. Before running the code, write your prediction for each packet P1 to P10: PASS or BLOCK, and which rule or mechanism decides.
  2. Run the simulation step by step and compare. Pause on P2: no WAN (Wide Area Network) rule exists, so what lets the reply in?
  3. Pause on P6: why does LAN-2 decide before LAN-5 is ever read?
  4. Record the ten decisions in the table produced by the code (ex1_packet_decisions.csv).

Deliverable reused later: the decision log with your predictions next to the observed results. In LAB_05 it becomes the model for your validation table: expected result, observed result, reason.

Code illustration of the real-life example

ex1_stateful_firewall.py

What this code does

The script simulates NM-FW01 in memory: it holds the rule table of five interfaces, processes ten packets in arrival order, checks the state table first, then reads the rules of the arrival interface from the top, stops at the first match, and applies default deny when nothing matches. It prints one decision line per packet and writes the decision log as a CSV (Comma-Separated Values) file.

How it relates to the lecture

Each line of the simulation corresponds to a concept of Lesson 1: forward_key and reverse_key build the 5-tuple, state_table is the state table, the for loop with break is first match, and the initial value BLOCK is default deny. Nothing is sent on a network.

76 {"id": "P8", "iface": "GUEST", "medium": "wireless, guest SSID", "who": "guest phone", "src": "192.168.40.23", "sport": 49152, "dst": "192.168.30.10", "dport": 445, "proto": "tcp", "flags": "SYN"},
77 # P9: the same guest phone opens an HTTPS website on the Internet.
78 {"id": "P9", "iface": "GUEST", "medium": "wireless, guest SSID", "who": "guest phone", "src": "192.168.40.23", "sport": 49153, "dst": "203.0.113.80", "dport": 443, "proto": "tcp", "flags": "SYN"},
79 # P10: the web server in the DMZ tries to open SMB on a user workstation, the typical next move after a web server compromise.
80 {"id": "P10", "iface": "DMZ", "medium": "DMZ server", "who": "NM-WEB01", "src": "192.168.20.10", "sport": 45000, "dst": "192.168.10.21", "dport": 445, "proto": "tcp", "flags": "SYN"},
81# The closing bracket ends the list that started above.
82]
83
84
85# addr_in answers one question: does this address belong to the address specification written in a rule?
86def addr_in(addr, spec):
87 # "any" in a rule matches every address, so the function can stop immediately.
88 if spec == "any":
89 # Returning True here means "the address matches this rule field".
90 return True
91 # Convert the text address into an address object so network membership can be tested exactly.
92 ip = ipaddress.ip_address(addr)
93 # in_private is True when the address sits in one of the three RFC 1918 ranges listed at the top.
94 in_private = any(ip in net for net in PRIVATE_NETS)
95 # The special word PRIVATE matches every private address (all internal zones at once).
96 if spec == "PRIVATE":
97 # Give back the private-range test result directly.
98 return in_private
99 # The special word !PRIVATE matches every public address, which is how a rule says "the Internet".
100 if spec == "!PRIVATE":
101 # The inverted test: public means "not private".
102 return not in_private
103 # Otherwise the rule names one host or one network; ip_network turns "192.168.30.10" into a one-address network.
104 return ip in ipaddress.ip_network(spec)
105
106
107# rule_matches checks the protocol, the source, the destination and the destination port of a packet against one rule.
108def rule_matches(rule, pkt):
109 # All four conditions must be true together; the first false condition stops the test.
110 return (
111 # Condition 1: the rule's protocol is "any" or equals the packet's protocol (tcp or udp).
112 rule["proto"] in ("any", pkt["proto"])
113 # Condition 2: the packet's source address fits the rule's source field.
114 and addr_in(pkt["src"], rule["src"])
115 # Condition 3: the packet's destination address fits the rule's destination field.
116 and addr_in(pkt["dst"], rule["dst"])
117 # Condition 4: the rule has no port list (all ports) or the destination port is in its list.
118 and (rule["ports"] is None or pkt["dport"] in rule["ports"])
119 # The closing parenthesis ends the expression that started above.
120 )
121
122
123# forward_key describes a connection as (protocol, source, source port, destination, destination port) in the direction it was opened.
124def forward_key(pkt):
125 # This five-part description is the 5-tuple the firewall stores in its state table.
126 return (pkt["proto"], pkt["src"], pkt["sport"], pkt["dst"], pkt["dport"])
127
128
129# reverse_key describes the same connection seen from the other side, which is what a reply packet looks like.
130def reverse_key(pkt):
131 # Source and destination are swapped: a reply travels from the server back to the client.
132 return (pkt["proto"], pkt["dst"], pkt["dport"], pkt["src"], pkt["sport"])
133
134
135# The state table starts empty: no connection has been allowed yet.
136state_table = []
137# The decision log collects one row per packet for the screen and for the CSV file.
138log = []
139
140# Print a title line so the output identifies the firewall and the method used.
141print("NM-FW01 stateful inspection, first match per interface, default deny")
142# Process the packets one at a time, in the order they arrive.
143for pkt in PACKETS:
144 # Step 1 of stateful inspection: is this packet a reply to a connection that is already in the state table?
145 if reverse_key(pkt) in state_table:
146 # It is a reply, so it passes without reading any rule; this is why no WAN rule is needed for return traffic.
147 decision, reason = "PASS", "state table (reply to an allowed connection)"
148 # Step 2: the packet opens something new, so the rules must decide.
149 else:
150 # Start from default deny: if no rule matches, this value stays.
151 decision, reason = "BLOCK", "default deny (no rule matched)"
152 # Read the rules from top to bottom.
153 for rule in RULES:
154 # A rule is considered only on the interface where the packet arrived, and only if all its fields match.
155 if rule["iface"] == pkt["iface"] and rule_matches(rule, pkt):
156 # First match: take this rule's action and remember which rule decided.
157 decision, reason = rule["action"], "rule " + rule["id"]
158 # Stop reading rules; lower rules are never evaluated for this packet.
159 break
160 # A new connection that was allowed is remembered, so its replies will pass in Step 1.
161 if decision == "PASS":
162 # Store the connection in the direction it was opened.
163 state_table.append(forward_key(pkt))
164 # Build the log row: packet, sender, medium, arrival interface, destination, decision and reason.
165 row = [pkt["id"], pkt["who"], pkt["medium"], pkt["iface"], pkt["dst"] + ":" + str(pkt["dport"]), decision, reason]
166 # Keep the row for the CSV file.
167 log.append(row)
168 # Print the row so the class can compare it with the prediction made before running.
169 print(f'{row[0]:<4} {row[1]:<12} {row[3]:<5} -> {row[4]:<18} {decision:<5} {reason}')
170
171# Open the evidence file; newline="" lets the csv module control line endings itself.
172with open("ex1_packet_decisions.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
173 # Create a writer that turns Python lists into CSV lines.
174 writer = csv.writer(handle)
175 # First line of the file: the column names.
176 writer.writerow(["packet", "sender", "medium", "arrival_interface", "destination", "decision", "reason"])
177 # Then one line per packet decision.
178 writer.writerows(log)
179
180# Summary line: how many packets passed, how many were blocked, and how many connections are tracked.
181print(f"{sum(r[5] == 'PASS' for r in log)} passed, {sum(r[5] == 'BLOCK' for r in log)} blocked, {len(state_table)} connections in the state table")
182

Step-by-step explanation of ex1_stateful_firewall.py
  1. Lines with import load two standard modules: csv for the output file and ipaddress to test network membership exactly.
  2. PRIVATE_NETS lists the three RFC (Request for Comments) 1918 ranges. A destination outside them is treated as the Internet, which is how the rules can say "Internet" without listing every public address.
  3. RULES is the rule table. Every rule has an interface, a source, a destination, a protocol, a port list and an action. The order inside each interface is the order of evaluation.
  4. PACKETS lists ten packets with their arrival interface and their 5-tuple. The field medium records how the sender is connected (wired, corporate SSID (Service Set Identifier), Internet, DMZ (Demilitarized Zone), guest SSID (Service Set Identifier)).
  5. addr_in compares one address with one rule field. It handles four cases: any, PRIVATE, !PRIVATE, and a named host or network.
  6. rule_matches combines four conditions with and. Python stops at the first false condition, exactly like a firewall stops comparing fields as soon as one does not fit.
  7. forward_key and reverse_key build the 5-tuple of a connection in its opening direction and in the reply direction.
  8. The main loop first asks whether the packet is a reply (reverse_key in state_table). P2 passes this way even though the WAN (Wide Area Network) interface has no rule for it.
  9. For a new connection, decision starts as BLOCK (default deny). The inner loop reads the rules; a rule counts only if it belongs to the arrival interface and all fields match. break implements first match.
  10. A passed connection is added to the state table, so its replies will be recognised.
  11. Each decision is printed and stored. At the end, the CSV (Comma-Separated Values) file is written and a summary counts passes, blocks and tracked connections: 6 passed, 4 blocked, 5 states.

Practice (no marks: the session plan has no quiz today)
Four multiple-choice and two multiple-select questions
Question 1 of 6. Multiple choice, one answer.
NM-WS01 opened an HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) connection to 203.0.113.80 and the LAN (Local Area Network) rule allowed it. The server's SYN-ACK (Synchronize-Acknowledgment) reply arrives on the WAN (Wide Area Network) interface, which has no rule for it. What does NM-FW01 do?
Show hint
Before reading any rule, a stateful firewall consults something else.
Show answer and explanations
Correct answer: b
  • a) Incorrect. Rules are read only for packets that match no state entry. This reply belongs to an allowed connection.
  • b) Correct. The first packet created a state entry; the reply matches it in the reverse direction and passes without any rule.
  • c) Incorrect. That broad rule is what a stateless filter would need, and it is exactly what stateful inspection avoids.
  • d) Incorrect. Reject is a rule action. No rule is involved for a packet that belongs to a tracked connection.
Question 2 of 6. Multiple choice, one answer.
On the LAN (Local Area Network) interface, rule 2 blocks the user zone from the firewall's management ports and rule 5 allows the user zone to reach HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) anywhere. A staff laptop opens https://192.168.10.1. Which rule decides?
Show hint
Count from the top and stop at the first rule that fits.
Show answer and explanations
Correct answer: d
  • a) Incorrect. Actions have no priority of their own; the position of the rule decides.
  • b) Incorrect. Only one rule is applied. Specificity matters only because you place specific rules higher.
  • c) Incorrect. Default deny applies only when no rule matches, and rule 2 matches.
  • d) Correct. With first match, rule 2 fits the packet (user zone, firewall address, port 443) and stops the evaluation.
Question 3 of 6. Multiple choice, one answer.
The access point NM-AP01 maps the staff SSID (Service Set Identifier) to VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) 10, the user zone. Which statement is correct?
Show hint
The firewall sees a VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) interface, not a radio.
Show answer and explanations
Correct answer: a
  • a) Correct. After the access point forwards its frames onto VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) 10, the laptop's traffic arrives on the LAN (Local Area Network) interface.
  • b) Incorrect. Only the link between laptop and access point is radio. Traffic between zones still crosses the firewall.
  • c) Incorrect. Rules are written per interface and per network, not per device.
  • d) Incorrect. WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3) protects the radio link and controls who joins. It does not decide what a client may reach.
Question 4 of 6. Multiple choice, one answer.
Which action is usually preferred on the Internet-facing (WAN (Wide Area Network)) interface for unwanted packets, and why?
Show hint
Think about what an Internet scanner learns from each answer.
Show answer and explanations
Correct answer: c
  • a) Incorrect. Reject sends extra packets back and confirms that something answers at that address.
  • b) Incorrect. Passing unwanted traffic contradicts default deny; detection does not replace filtering.
  • c) Correct. A silent drop leaves the scanner waiting for a timeout and reveals nothing.
  • d) Incorrect. Stateful inspection works with any action; the action only changes the answer sent to the source.
Question 5 of 6. Multiple select, several answers.
Which statements about stateful network firewalls are correct? (Select 3)
Show hint
Three statements describe the state table, rule order and default behaviour correctly.
Show answer and explanations
Correct answer: b, c, d
  • a) Incorrect. They are complementary layers of defense in depth.
  • b) Correct. Replies match the state table.
  • c) Correct. Protocol, source address, source port, destination address and destination port identify the connection.
  • d) Correct. That is the implicit last rule of every interface.
  • e) Incorrect. Only the rules of the arrival interface are evaluated.
  • f) Incorrect. Every entry has a timeout; idle or closed connections are removed.
Question 6 of 6. Multiple select, several answers.
NorthMaple will add a guest Wi-Fi at Class 13. Which measures belong to a correct guest design? (Select 3)
Show hint
Separate the guests, give them the Internet only, and stop them from reaching each other.
Show answer and explanations
Correct answer: a, b, c
  • a) Correct. A separate interface lets the firewall apply guest-only rules.
  • b) Correct. Guests need web access, never the company's zones.
  • c) Correct. Guest devices cannot reach each other on the same SSID (Service Set Identifier).
  • d) Incorrect. Sharing credentials merges the two groups and makes the staff passphrase public.
  • e) Incorrect. VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) 10 is the user zone; guests would receive staff access.
  • f) Incorrect. Management of network devices stays restricted to NM-LWS01.
Lesson 2 of 4, about 14 minutes
Translating the zoning design of LAB_01 into real firewall rules between zones
Slide 17Translating the zoning design of LAB_01 into real firewall rules between zones
Terms to learn in this lesson
Zoning table
The LAB_01 deliverable: one row per allowed or denied flow, with source zone, destination zone, service or protocol, and a one- or two-sentence justification.
Ingress interface
The firewall interface through which a packet enters. On pfSense and OPNsense, a rule is placed on the ingress interface of the traffic it controls.
Alias
A named object on the firewall (host, network or port list) used in rules instead of raw numbers, for example NM_FS01 or LAN_NET.
Inverted match
A rule field that matches everything except the listed value; "destination not PRIVATE" is how a rule targets the Internet.
Rule shadowing
A rule that can never match because a broader rule above it always matches first. The lower rule exists but does nothing.
Traceability
Every rule refers to one zoning row, and every zoning row has at least one rule; the rule description carries the row identifier.
Port forward
Destination NAT (Network Address Translation) on the WAN (Wide Area Network) interface that sends traffic for a public address and port to a private host, such as NM-WEB01 in the DMZ (Demilitarized Zone).
Positive and negative test
A positive test proves an allowed flow works; a negative test proves a forbidden flow is blocked. Both are needed to validate a rule.


The zoning table you wrote in Class 2 is a specification: it states which flows the business needs and why. A firewall rule set is its implementation. This lesson gives you a repeatable method to go from one to the other, so that nothing is allowed that the table does not justify, and nothing the table justifies is forgotten.


Slide 18The zoning table is the specification
2.1 The starting point: your zoning table


Each row of the zoning table has a source zone, a destination zone, a service with its protocol and port, and a justification. Rows that forbid a flow are just as useful as rows that allow one, because they become explicit, logged block rules. The reference table used today has twelve rows, Z1 to Z12 (Table 3). Figure 4, after Example 2, shows the same rows as a zone-to-zone matrix: every cell is either allowed by a named row, explicitly blocked, or closed by default deny.

Z3User zoneLAN_NETInternet!PRIVATEtcp443ALLOWStaff need encrypted web access to the Internet.

Teaching set. In LAB_05 you translate the rows of your own Class 2 zoning table.


Slide 19Seven steps from a zoning row to a rule (1/2)
2.2 Seven steps from a row to a rule


    

  1. Map each zone to an interface. Internet to WAN (Wide Area Network), user zone to LAN (Local Area Network), DMZ (Demilitarized Zone) to the DMZ (Demilitarized Zone) interface, server zone to SERVERS. Rename the optional interfaces (OPT1, OPT2) with the zone names, so the rule set reads like the design.
    2. 

  2. Create aliases. Define NM_WEB01, NM_FS01, NM_LWS01 and NM_FW01 as hosts, LAN_NET, DMZ_NET and SRV_NET as networks, and PRIVATE as the three RFC (Request for Comments) 1918 ranges (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1918). An alias is a named object; when an address changes, you change the alias once and every rule follows.
    3. 

  3. Place each rule on the ingress interface. The rule goes on the interface where the traffic enters the firewall, which is the interface of the source zone. Z2 (user zone to file server) lives on LAN (Local Area Network), not on SERVERS. Figure 3 shows why: the request never enters through SERVERS, so a rule there would never be read. The reply needs no rule, because the state table returns it.
    4. 

  4. Write the narrowest rule that satisfies the row. Specify the protocol, the source, the destination and the port. "The Internet" is not "any": on an internal interface, "any" also includes every other zone. Use the inverted alias, destination not PRIVATE, so that a rule for Internet browsing cannot reach the DMZ (Demilitarized Zone) or the server zone by accident.
    5. 

  5. Slide 20Seven steps from a zoning row to a rule (2/2)
    Order the rules on each interface. Put management of the firewall from NM-LWS01 first, so an error lower in the list can never lock the administrator out. Then the narrow allows toward one named host, then the explicit blocks, then the broad allows. Specific before general prevents rule shadowing: a broad rule placed above a narrow one would match first, and the narrow rule would never act.
    6. 

  6. Write the description. Start every description with the zoning row identifier: "Z2 Accountants open client records". This gives traceability in both directions: from a rule you can find its justification, and from a zoning row you can find its rule.
    7. 

  7. Publish the DMZ (Demilitarized Zone) service. When the DMZ (Demilitarized Zone) uses private addresses, Internet visitors reach NM-WEB01 through a port forward on WAN (Wide Area Network) (destination NAT (Network Address Translation) from the WAN (Wide Area Network) address, port 443, to 192.168.20.10). pfSense and OPNsense filter after the address translation, so the matching WAN (Wide Area Network) rule names the internal destination NM_WEB01. In a lab where the WAN (Wide Area Network) side is itself a lab network, you may route to the DMZ (Demilitarized Zone) directly; document which method you used.
    8. 



Slide 21Place the rule where the traffic enters


Slide 22Specific before general: avoiding rule shadowing
Applied to the reference table, the method produces the rule set of Table 5 below Example 2: two rules on WAN (Wide Area Network), six on LAN (Local Area Network), three on DMZ (Demilitarized Zone) and one on SERVERS, each followed by the implicit default deny. Notice Z12: the web server needs DNS (Domain Name System) to find its update servers. Because it is a narrow allow toward one address, it sits above the DMZ (Demilitarized Zone) block Z9. If it were placed below, Z9 would shadow it and the web server would silently stop updating.


Slide 23Prove every rule: positive and negative tests
2.3 Validating every rule with allowed and blocked tests


LAB_05 asks you to prove every rule, not to assume it. For each allowed row, run a positive test from a machine in the source zone to the destination port. For each forbidden row, and for the ports an allowed rule must not open, run a negative test. NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP 800-41 Rev. 1 treats this testing as part of the firewall policy life cycle (https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/41/r1/final). Record four things per test: the command, the expected result, the observed result and the evidence (a screenshot and, for blocks, the firewall log line).


    

  • On Linux: nc -zv -w 3 192.168.30.10 445 (-z: open and close without sending data, -v: print the result, -w 3: give up after 3 seconds).
    • 

  • On Windows: Test-NetConnection 192.168.30.10 -Port 445, then read the line TcpTestSucceeded.
    • 

  • For DNS (Domain Name System) (UDP (User Datagram Protocol) 53): nslookup www.northmaple.lab 192.168.10.1, because a TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) port check does not test a UDP (User Datagram Protocol) service.
    • 

  • On the firewall: the live firewall log (Firewall, Log Files, Live View on OPNsense; Status, System Logs, Firewall on pfSense) shows which rule passed or blocked each attempt.
    • 



Slide 24Reading a test result
Table 4. Reading the result of a connection test
What you observeWhat it usually meansHow to confirmVerdict for a positive testVerdict for a negative test
Succeeded / TcpTestSucceeded : TrueThe firewall passed the packet and a service answeredPass line in the firewall logPASSFAIL: the rule is too wide
Timeout after the waiting periodDropped by a block rule, default deny, or a host firewallBlock line in the firewall log, or none (then check the host)FAIL: find the missing rulePASS if the log shows the expected block
Connection refused, immediatelyReject rule, or the host received it and nothing listensFirewall log: reject line, or pass line (then the host refused)FAIL: service down or reject rulePASS only with a reject line in the log
Name resolved (nslookup answer)DNS (Domain Name System) reached the resolver and it answeredPass line for UDP (User Datagram Protocol) 53 in the logPASSFAIL: the resolver is reachable
The firewall log is the arbiter. Keep its screenshot with every negative test.


Read results carefully. A timeout means the packet was dropped somewhere. "Connection refused" can mean a reject rule, but it can also mean the firewall passed the packet and the destination host had no service listening, which is a failed negative test. When a positive test fails, remember the host firewalls of LAB_03: Windows Defender Firewall on NM-FS01 may be the layer that refuses SMB (Server Message Block). The firewall log separates the two cases.


Slide 25Seven mistakes found in most first rule sets
2.4 Mistakes that appear in almost every first rule set


A rule "any to any" left from the installation; a rule placed on the destination interface instead of the ingress interface; "any" used where "the Internet" was meant; a missing DNS (Domain Name System) rule that makes every web test fail; a narrow rule shadowed by a broad one; blocks without logging, which leave you with no evidence; and descriptions that say "test" instead of naming the zoning row. Each of these costs points in Chapter 5 of the Final Project, because the checklist grades the rule set, its validation and its justification separately.

Slide 27Example 2: from zoning rows to rule set and test plan
Real-life example, Lesson 2
From NorthMaple's zoning table to the LAB_05 rule set and test plan
Task of this example
Convert the twelve rows of the reference zoning table into an ordered rule set for NM-FW01 (per interface), check that every row produced a rule, and generate the list of allowed and blocked tests that LAB_05 part 2 requires.
How it relates to this lesson
The example executes the seven steps of section 2.2 and the test logic of section 2.3: zone-to-interface mapping, aliases, ingress placement, ordering against shadowing, traceable descriptions, and positive plus negative tests.
Where this example and its deliverable return in the scheduled labs
  • LAB_05 part 2 (today): the two CSV (Comma-Separated Values) files are the skeleton of your firewall rule set and your validation evidence for Chapter 5.
  • Class 13: the guest zone adds rows (guest to Internet, guest to PRIVATE blocked) that you run through the same method.
  • LAB_06 (Classes 16-17): the VPN (Virtual Private Network) adds a WAN (Wide Area Network) row for the WireGuard port and rules on the VPN (Virtual Private Network) interface, translated the same way.
  • Class 18: the traceability check is the fastest way to build your gap list for the Final Project assembly.


The IT (Information Technology) administrator of NorthMaple prints the zoning table approved in Class 2 and must turn it into rules before Monday. Typing rules one by one in the web interface, in whatever order they come to mind, is how shadowed rules and forgotten rows appear. Instead, the administrator applies the method mechanically: map, alias, place, order, describe, and plan the tests.


    

  1. Replace the ZONING rows in the script with the rows of your own Class 2 table (keep the same columns).
    2. 

  2. Run the script and read the ordering: why does Z12 come before Z9 on the DMZ (Demilitarized Zone) interface?
    3. 

  3. Open LAB05_rule_set.csv: this is the order in which you create the rules on NM-FW01.
    4. 

  4. Open LAB05_test_plan.csv: run each command from the named machine and fill the observed and evidence columns.
    5. 



Deliverable reused later: LAB05_rule_set.csv and LAB05_test_plan.csv, completed with your observations, are the rule-set and validation evidence of Chapter 5 of the Final Project and of Chapter 5 of the Course Procedure Manual.


Code illustration of the real-life example
ex2_zoning_to_rules.py
What this code does
The script reads the zoning table as data, assigns each row a priority group, sorts the rows, places each rule on the interface of the source zone, generates positive tests for allowed rows, negative tests for denied rows and an SSH (Secure Shell) negative test for narrow allows, performs a two-way traceability check, and writes the rule set and the test plan as CSV (Comma-Separated Values) files.
How it relates to the lecture
This is section 2.2 as code: ZONE_IFACE is step 1, ALIASES step 2, iface = ZONE_IFACE[szone] step 3, the inverted !PRIVATE destination step 4, priority() step 5, descr with the row identifier step 6. The tests list is section 2.3.
Python 3ex2_zoning_to_rules.py
This player needs JavaScript: open the saved file in a browser. The complete source code is shown below and can be read without it.
Orange line: the line that just ran. The trace was recorded from a real run of this exact file.
Source code: every line of code has its comment above it
1# ============================================================================
2# ex2_zoning_to_rules.py - Class 12, Lesson 2: Translating the LAB_01 zoning design into firewall rules
3# Cyber Defense 420-D03-AB - Cyber.SoHo - educational use inside an isolated laboratory only.
4#
5# Task: read the zoning table of NorthMaple Accounting Inc. (the Class 2 deliverable of LAB_01),
6# place every row on the firewall interface where its traffic ENTERS NM-FW01, order the rules
7# on each interface (management first, explicit blocks next, narrow allows, broad allows last),
8# check that every zoning row became a rule, and write the allowed/blocked test plan that
9# LAB_05 part 2 asks you to execute and document.
10#
11# Output: LAB05_rule_set.csv and LAB05_test_plan.csv (Chapter 5 of the Final Project and of
12# the Course Procedure Manual). The zoning rows below are the class reference set: replace
13# them with the rows of YOUR own Class 2 zoning table before you use the output in LAB_05.
14# Abbreviations: DMZ (Demilitarized Zone), LAN (Local Area Network), WAN (Wide Area Network),
15# HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure), SMB (Server Message Block), SSH (Secure Shell),
16# DNS (Domain Name System), TCP (Transmission Control Protocol), UDP (User Datagram Protocol),
17# CSV (Comma-Separated Values).
18# Runs with the Python 3 standard library only. It sends no network traffic at all.
19# ============================================================================
20 
21# csv writes the rule set and the test plan so they open directly in the LAB_05 workbook.
22import csv
23 
24# Which firewall interface each zone is connected to. Traffic from a zone ENTERS the firewall on that interface.
25ZONE_IFACE = {"Internet": "WAN", "DMZ": "DMZ", "User zone": "LAN", "Server zone": "SERVERS"}
26# Names (aliases) for hosts and networks, so rules read like the zoning table instead of like raw addresses.
27ALIASES = {"NM_WEB01": "192.168.20.10", "NM_FS01": "192.168.30.10", "NM_LWS01": "192.168.10.5", "NM_FW01": "192.168.10.1",
28           "NM_FW01_DMZ": "192.168.20.1", "LAN_NET": "192.168.10.0/24", "DMZ_NET": "192.168.20.0/24", "SRV_NET": "192.168.30.0/24",
29           "INTERNAL_NETS": "192.168.10.0/24 192.168.30.0/24"}
30# For rows whose destination is a whole range, the test needs one real example address inside that range.
31TEST_TARGET = {"PRIVATE": "192.168.10.21", "INTERNAL_NETS": "192.168.10.21", "!PRIVATE": "203.0.113.80"}
32# The machine used to run each test, and the tool that fits its operating system (nc on Linux, Test-NetConnection on Windows).
33TEST_HOST = {"NM_LWS01": ("NM-LWS01", "linux"), "LAN_NET": ("NM-WS01", "windows"), "DMZ_NET": ("NM-WEB01", "linux"),
34             "SRV_NET": ("NM-FS01", "linux"), "any": ("WAN test client", "linux")}
35 
36# The zoning table: id, source zone, source, destination zone, destination, protocol, ports, action, justification.
37ZONING = [
38    # Z1: visitors on the Internet reach the public website, and only on HTTPS.
39    ("Z1", "Internet", "any", "DMZ", "NM_WEB01", "tcp", "443", "ALLOW", "Visitors must reach the public website; nothing else in the DMZ is published."),
40    # Z2: staff open client records on the file server over SMB.
41    ("Z2", "User zone", "LAN_NET", "Server zone", "NM_FS01", "tcp", "445", "ALLOW", "Accountants open client records stored on the file server."),
42    # Z3: staff browse the web and use cloud services over encrypted connections.
43    ("Z3", "User zone", "LAN_NET", "Internet", "!PRIVATE", "tcp", "443", "ALLOW", "Staff need encrypted web access to the Internet."),
44    # Z4: workstations resolve names only through the firewall's resolver.
45    ("Z4", "User zone", "LAN_NET", "Firewall", "NM_FW01", "udp", "53", "ALLOW", "One controlled resolver; no workstation talks to outside DNS servers."),
46    # Z5: only the IT administrator's workstation manages the firewall (decided in Class 11).
47    ("Z5", "User zone", "NM_LWS01", "Firewall", "NM_FW01", "tcp", "443,22", "ALLOW", "Management of NM-FW01 is limited to NM-LWS01."),
48    # Z6: the administrator workstation administers the Linux servers over SSH.
49    ("Z6", "User zone", "NM_LWS01", "Server zone", "NM_FS01", "tcp", "22", "ALLOW", "The administrator maintains the file server over SSH."),
50    # Z7: the servers download their security updates.
51    ("Z7", "Server zone", "SRV_NET", "Internet", "!PRIVATE", "tcp", "443", "ALLOW", "Servers must receive security updates."),
52    # Z8: the public web server downloads its security updates.
53    ("Z8", "DMZ", "DMZ_NET", "Internet", "!PRIVATE", "tcp", "443", "ALLOW", "The web server must receive security updates."),
54    # Z9: the DMZ never opens connections toward the internal zones.
55    ("Z9", "DMZ", "DMZ_NET", "Internal zones", "PRIVATE", "any", "any", "DENY", "A compromised public server must not reach internal systems."),
56    # Z10: nobody on the Internet opens connections to the user zone or the server zone (the DMZ is excluded on purpose, see Z1).
57    ("Z10", "Internet", "any", "Internal zones", "INTERNAL_NETS", "any", "any", "DENY", "Internal zones accept no connection that starts on the Internet."),
58    # Z11: other user-zone machines may not open the firewall's management ports.
59    ("Z11", "User zone", "LAN_NET", "Firewall", "NM_FW01", "tcp", "443,22", "DENY", "Only NM-LWS01 manages the firewall."),
60    # Z12: the web server resolves names through the firewall's DMZ address; without DNS it could not find its update servers.
61    ("Z12", "DMZ", "DMZ_NET", "Firewall", "NM_FW01_DMZ", "udp", "53", "ALLOW", "The web server needs name resolution to download its updates."),
62# The closing bracket ends the list that started above.
63]
64 
65 
66# priority gives each rule a group number; rules are later sorted by it, so the order no longer depends on typing order.
67def priority(row):
68    # Unpack the fields of the zoning row that decide the group.
69    zid, szone, src, dzone, dst, proto, ports, action, why = row
70    # Group 1: management of the firewall from one named host, so the administrator can never be locked out.
71    if dst == "NM_FW01" and src == "NM_LWS01":
72        # Lowest number means the rule is placed first on its interface.
73        return 1
74    # Group 2: narrow allows toward one named host; specific rules go first so a broader block cannot hide a precise need (Z12).
75    if action == "ALLOW" and dst in ALIASES and "/" not in ALIASES[dst]:
76        # Narrow allows come right after management.
77        return 2
78    # Group 3: explicit blocks, placed above the broad allows so a broad allow can never open what the table forbids.
79    if action == "DENY":
80        # Logged blocks come before the broad allows.
81        return 3
82    # Group 4: allows toward a whole network or toward "the Internet" (broad rules) go last.
83    return 4
84 
85 
86# Rules are collected per interface, because a firewall evaluates only the rules of the interface a packet arrives on.
87rules = {"WAN": [], "LAN": [], "DMZ": [], "SERVERS": []}
88# The test plan collects one planned connection test per line.
89tests = []
90 
91# Print a title so the output identifies what is being built.
92print("Translating the zoning table of NorthMaple Accounting Inc. into NM-FW01 rules")
93# Sort the zoning rows by priority; sorted keeps the original Z-order inside each group.
94for row in sorted(ZONING, key=priority):
95    # Unpack the row into readable names.
96    zid, szone, src, dzone, dst, proto, ports, action, why = row
97    # The rule goes on the interface of the SOURCE zone: that is where the traffic enters the firewall.
98    iface = ZONE_IFACE[szone]
99    # Translate the zoning action into the firewall action; blocks are logged so the firewall log can prove them.
100    fw_action, log_it = ("pass", "no") if action == "ALLOW" else ("block", "yes")
101    # Build the rule; the description starts with the zoning id, which gives two-way traceability.
102    rule = {"iface": iface, "action": fw_action, "proto": proto, "src": src, "dst": dst, "ports": ports, "log": log_it, "descr": zid + " " + why}
103    # Add the rule at the end of its interface list; the sort above already placed it in the right group.
104    rules[iface].append(rule)
105    # Pick the machine that will run the tests for this row, and its operating system.
106    host, os_name = TEST_HOST[src]
107    # A destination range gets its example address; a named host is translated to its own address.
108    target = TEST_TARGET.get(dst, ALIASES.get(dst))
109    # A row with "any" port is tested on SMB 445, a service internal machines really offer.
110    port_list = ["445"] if ports == "any" else ports.split(",")
111    # One test per port of the row: an ALLOW row expects a working connection, a DENY row expects a blocked one.
112    for port in port_list:
113        # Windows machines test with Test-NetConnection; Linux machines with nc (-z: no data, -v: verbose, -w 3: 3-second timeout).
114        tool = f"Test-NetConnection {target} -Port {port}" if os_name == "windows" else f"nc -zv -w 3 {target} {port}"
115        # UDP 53 cannot be tested with a TCP port check, so the test becomes a real name lookup through the firewall.
116        if proto == "udp":
117            # nslookup sends one DNS query for the website name to the resolver 192.168.10.1.
118            tool = f"nslookup www.northmaple.lab {target}"
119        # Record the planned test; observed and evidence stay empty until you run it in LAB_05.
120        tests.append([f"T{len(tests) + 1:02d}", zid, host, szone, f"{target}:{port}/{proto}", "ALLOW" if action == "ALLOW" else "BLOCK", tool, "", ""])
121    # Over-permission check: a narrow allow toward one server from a non-admin source must NOT open SSH (22) as a side effect.
122    if action == "ALLOW" and src != "NM_LWS01" and dst in ALIASES and dst != "NM_FW01" and "22" not in ports:
123        # The negative test uses the same tool family as the positive test, but on port 22.
124        neg_tool = f"Test-NetConnection {target} -Port 22" if os_name == "windows" else f"nc -zv -w 3 {target} 22"
125        # This test expects BLOCK; if it connects, the rule is wider than the zoning table says.
126        tests.append([f"T{len(tests) + 1:02d}", zid + "-neg", host, szone, f"{target}:22/tcp", "BLOCK", neg_tool, "", ""])
127    # Show progress: which zoning row produced which rule on which interface.
128    print(f"{zid:<4} -> {iface:<8} {fw_action:<5} {proto:<4} {src:>9} -> {dst:<9} port {ports}")
129 
130# Two-way traceability, direction 1: collect the zoning ids that appear in rule descriptions.
131used = {r["descr"].split()[0] for iface_rules in rules.values() for r in iface_rules}
132# Direction 2: any zoning row without a rule is a gap you would have to fix before LAB_05 validation.
133missing = [row[0] for row in ZONING if row[0] not in used]
134# Report the result of the traceability check.
135print("Traceability:", "every zoning row has a rule" if not missing else f"rows without a rule: {missing}")
136 
137# Write the rule set, interface by interface and in evaluation order, for the Chapter 5 rule-set evidence.
138with open("LAB05_rule_set.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
139    # The writer converts each list into one CSV line.
140    writer = csv.writer(handle)
141    # Column names first; "order" is the position of the rule on its interface.
142    writer.writerow(["interface", "order", "action", "protocol", "source", "destination", "ports", "log", "description"])
143    # Loop over the interfaces in a fixed order.
144    for iface, iface_rules in rules.items():
145        # enumerate numbers the rules 1, 2, 3 in the order the firewall reads them.
146        for order, r in enumerate(iface_rules, start=1):
147            # One line per rule.
148            writer.writerow([iface, order, r["action"], r["proto"], r["src"], r["dst"], r["ports"], r["log"], r["descr"]])
149        # Every interface ends with the implicit default deny; writing it down makes the evidence complete.
150        writer.writerow([iface, len(iface_rules) + 1, "block", "any", "any", "any", "any", "yes", "Default deny (implicit)"])
151 
152# Write the test plan; the two empty columns are filled in during LAB_05 with the observed result and the screenshot name.
153with open("LAB05_test_plan.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
154    # Writer for the test plan file.
155    writer = csv.writer(handle)
156    # Column names of the test plan.
157    writer.writerow(["test", "zoning_row", "run_from", "source_zone", "target", "expected", "command", "observed", "evidence"])
158    # One line per planned test.
159    writer.writerows(tests)
160 
161# Final summary: how many rules per interface and how many tests are planned.
162print("Rules per interface:", {k: len(v) for k, v in rules.items()}, "| planned tests:", len(tests))
163

Step-by-step explanation of ex2_zoning_to_rules.py
  1. ZONE_IFACE maps each zone to the interface where its traffic enters NM-FW01. ALIASES gives names to hosts and networks, and TEST_TARGET gives one example address for rows whose destination is a whole range.
  2. TEST_HOST chooses the machine that runs each test and its operating system, so the plan proposes nc on Linux and Test-NetConnection on Windows.
  3. ZONING holds the twelve rows. Each is a tuple: identifier, source zone, source, destination zone, destination, protocol, ports, action, justification.
  4. priority() returns a group number: 1 for management from NM-LWS01, 2 for narrow allows to one host, 3 for explicit blocks, 4 for broad allows. Sorting by this number is the ordering rule of step 5.
  5. The main loop takes the rows in sorted order. iface = ZONE_IFACE[szone] places the rule on the ingress interface (step 3).
  6. fw_action and log_it translate ALLOW into pass without logging and DENY into block with logging, so every block leaves evidence.
  7. The rule dictionary stores the fields and a description that starts with the zoning identifier (traceability, step 6).
  8. For each port of the row, one test line is created with the expected result (ALLOW or BLOCK) and the exact command to type. UDP (User Datagram Protocol) 53 is tested with nslookup instead of a port check.
  9. The over-permission check adds a negative SSH (Secure Shell) test for narrow allows from non-administrator sources: Z1-neg, Z2-neg and Z12-neg prove the rule opened only its own port.
  10. The traceability check collects the identifiers used in descriptions and lists any zoning row without a rule. The reference table prints "every zoning row has a rule".
  11. Two CSV (Comma-Separated Values) files are written: the rule set in evaluation order with the implicit default deny at the end of each interface, and the test plan with empty observed and evidence columns for LAB_05.

Four multiple-choice and two multiple-select questions
Question 1 of 6. Multiple choice, one answer.
Zoning row Z7 allows the server zone to download updates over HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) from the Internet. On which interface of NM-FW01 is the pass rule created?
Show hint
Where does the first packet of the update download enter the firewall?
Show answer and explanations
Correct answer: c
  • a) Incorrect. WAN (Wide Area Network) is the egress interface for this flow; rules are placed where traffic enters.
  • b) Incorrect. Each internal zone has its own interface and its own rules.
  • c) Correct. The request starts on NM-FS01 and enters the firewall through SERVERS.
  • d) Incorrect. The reply is handled by the state table; one rule on the ingress interface is enough.
Question 2 of 6. Multiple choice, one answer.
On the DMZ (Demilitarized Zone) interface, a block rule "DMZ_NET to PRIVATE" sits above a pass rule "DMZ_NET to NM_FW01_DMZ, UDP (User Datagram Protocol) 53". What is the effect?
Show hint
NM_FW01_DMZ (192.168.20.1) is a private address.
Show answer and explanations
Correct answer: a
  • a) Correct. The firewall's DMZ (Demilitarized Zone) address is inside PRIVATE, so the block decides before the DNS (Domain Name System) rule is read.
  • b) Incorrect. Order decides, not the action type.
  • c) Incorrect. Only one rule acts under first match.
  • d) Incorrect. The block rule has protocol any, so it covers UDP (User Datagram Protocol) as well.
Question 3 of 6. Multiple choice, one answer.
Which destination should the user-zone rule for Internet browsing (Z3) use on the LAN (Local Area Network) interface?
Show hint
The rule must reach public addresses and nothing internal.
Show answer and explanations
Correct answer: d
  • a) Incorrect. any includes the DMZ (Demilitarized Zone), the server zone and the firewall; the rule would open all of them on 443.
  • b) Incorrect. That is the firewall itself, not the websites staff want to reach.
  • c) Incorrect. LAN_NET is the source of the flow, not its destination.
  • d) Correct. The rule then reaches every public address and no internal zone.
Question 4 of 6. Multiple choice, one answer.
Why is the rule that lets NM-LWS01 manage the firewall placed first on the LAN (Local Area Network) interface?
Show hint
Think about what happens if a lower rule is written wrongly.
Show answer and explanations
Correct answer: b
  • a) Incorrect. Encryption does not change the order of evaluation.
  • b) Correct. With first match, the management rule always decides before any other LAN (Local Area Network) rule.
  • c) Incorrect. The appliances do not enforce this; it is a design decision (and an anti-lockout rule exists by default).
  • d) Incorrect. Logging is a per-rule option, independent of position.
Question 5 of 6. Multiple select, several answers.
Which elements must a LAB_05 validation record contain for each test? (Select 4)
Show hint
A colleague must be able to repeat the test and judge its result.
Show answer and explanations
Correct answer: a, c, e, f
  • a) Correct. Evidence proves the test really happened and shows which rule acted.
  • b) Incorrect. Hardware addresses belong to the device registry, not to the test record.
  • c) Correct. Without it, the observation cannot be judged.
  • d) Incorrect. Credentials never appear in documentation.
  • e) Correct. It makes the test reproducible.
  • f) Correct. Expected and observed are compared to decide pass or fail.
Question 6 of 6. Multiple select, several answers.
Which of these are typical mistakes in a first rule set? (Select 3)
Show hint
Look for rules that are too broad, misplaced, or impossible to prove.
Show answer and explanations
Correct answer: a, b, c
  • a) Correct. The validation evidence of Chapter 5 needs the log lines.
  • b) Correct. The rule is never read for that traffic.
  • c) Correct. It makes every specific LAN (Local Area Network) rule meaningless.
  • d) Incorrect. Negative tests are required to prove a rule is not wider than intended.
  • e) Incorrect. Aliases make rules readable and easy to maintain.
  • f) Incorrect. That is good practice: it provides traceability.
Lesson 3 of 4, about 13 minutes
Techniques and tools for session hijacking prevention and cache protection (introductory level)
Slide 31Session hijacking prevention and cache protection (introductory level)
Terms to learn in this lesson
Session
The period during which a server recognises an authenticated user without asking for the password again.
Session identifier (session ID (Identifier))
A random value the server issues after login and the browser returns with every request, usually inside a cookie.
Session hijacking
Taking over a valid session by obtaining or imposing its identifier; the server then treats the attacker as the user.
On-path attack
An attack in which the adversary places a system between two communicating parties to read or change their traffic (formerly called man-in-the-middle).
ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) cache
The table in which a host keeps the MAC (Media Access Control) address it has learned for each IP (Internet Protocol) address of its local network.
ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) cache poisoning
Sending forged ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) replies so that a host stores the attacker's MAC (Media Access Control) address for another IP (Internet Protocol) address, typically the gateway.
DNS (Domain Name System) cache poisoning
Inserting a forged answer into a resolver's cache, so that clients receive a wrong address for a name until the entry expires.
DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions)
Signatures added to DNS (Domain Name System) records; a validating resolver checks them and marks verified answers with the AD (Authenticated Data) flag.
Cookie attributes Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite
Secure: sent only over HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure). HttpOnly: not readable by scripts in the page. SameSite: not attached to requests started by other sites.
HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security)
A response header that tells the browser to contact this site only over HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) for a stated period.
Cache-Control: no-store
A response directive that forbids the browser and any intermediate cache from keeping a copy of the page.


After a user logs in to a web application, the server does not ask for the password with every click. It issues a session identifier, and whoever presents that identifier is treated as the logged-in user. This lesson explains how attackers obtain session identifiers, which network and application controls prevent it, and why the caches that computers keep (ARP (Address Resolution Protocol), DNS (Domain Name System) and web caches) are part of the problem.


Slide 32How a session works, and what hijacking takes
3.1 How a session works and what hijacking means


At login, the server creates a random session ID (Identifier), stores it with the user's identity, and sends it to the browser in a Set-Cookie header. The browser returns the cookie with every following request. Session hijacking is the takeover of that session: an attacker who obtains the identifier sends it with their own requests and receives the user's access, without ever knowing the password. Multi-factor authentication at login does not help once the session exists, because the cookie is issued after the authentication step.


Slide 33Four paths to a session identifier
At the network level, older attacks predicted TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) sequence numbers to inject packets into an open connection; modern operating systems choose random initial sequence numbers, and encryption makes injected data useless, so this form is rare today. At the application level, the attacker simply needs a copy of the cookie. There are four common ways to obtain it, shown in Figure 5: reading unencrypted traffic from an on-path position (on the LAN (Local Area Network) through ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) cache poisoning, or on Wi-Fi through a rogue access point), sending the victim to a lookalike server through DNS (Domain Name System) cache poisoning, running a script inside the page through cross-site scripting (XSS), or reading it from an infected endpoint. A fifth technique, session fixation, works the other way round: the attacker makes the victim log in with an identifier the attacker already knows.



Slide 34Six controls against session hijacking
3.2 Preventing session hijacking at the application and transport level


    

  1. HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) for every page, not only the login page. TLS (Transport Layer Security) encrypts the whole request, including the cookie, so an on-path host sees only ciphertext.
    2. 

  2. The Secure attribute on the session cookie. The browser then never sends the cookie over plain HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol), even if a link or a redirection tries to.
    3. 

  3. HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security). The Strict-Transport-Security header makes the browser refuse plain HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) for the site for a stated period, which defeats attempts to downgrade the first connection.
    4. 

  4. The HttpOnly attribute. Scripts running in the page cannot read the cookie, which removes the most common use of an XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) flaw.
    5. 

  5. The SameSite attribute (Lax or Strict). The browser does not attach the cookie to requests started by another site, which also reduces cross-site request forgery (CSRF).
    6. 

  6. A new identifier after login, and server-side expiry. Regenerating the ID (Identifier) at authentication defeats fixation. An idle timeout, an absolute timeout and a logout that destroys the session on the server limit the time a stolen ID (Identifier) is useful. The OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) Session Management Cheat Sheet recommends identifiers with at least 64 bits of entropy and never placing them in URLs (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Session_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html).
    7. 



Slide 35Cookie attributes and security headers
Table 7. Session cookie attributes and security headers
SettingWhere it is setWhat it preventsChecked by Example 3
SecureSet-Cookie attributeCookie sent over unencrypted HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) and read on the pathYes (FAIL if missing)
HttpOnlySet-Cookie attributeCookie read by a script in the page (XSS (Cross-Site Scripting))Yes (FAIL if missing)
SameSite=Lax or StrictSet-Cookie attributeCookie attached to requests started by other sites (CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery))Yes (WARN if missing)
Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security))Response headerDowngrade of the first connection to plain HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol)Yes (WARN if missing)
Cache-Control: no-storeResponse headerAuthenticated page kept by the browser or a shared cacheYes (WARN if missing)
New ID (Identifier) after login, idle and absolute timeoutsApplication logic on the serverFixation; long use of a stolen identifierNo (review the application)
Sources: RFC (Request for Comments) 6265 (cookies), RFC (Request for Comments) 6797 (HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security)), RFC (Request for Comments) 9111 (HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) caching), OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) Session Management Cheat Sheet.


Slide 36ARP cache poisoning and its defenses
3.3 Cache protection: the ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) cache


To send a packet to another host on the same LAN (Local Area Network), a computer needs that host's MAC (Media Access Control) address. It asks with an ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) request ("who has 192.168.10.1?") and stores the answer in its ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) cache. ARP (Address Resolution Protocol), defined in RFC (Request for Comments) 826 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc826), has no authentication: a host accepts replies it never asked for and overwrites the entry. In ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) cache poisoning, an attacker on the same LAN (Local Area Network) repeatedly announces "192.168.10.1 is at my MAC (Media Access Control) address". The victim then sends its traffic for the gateway to the attacker, who forwards it and reads it on the way (Figure 6, after Example 3).


Defenses work at several layers. Dynamic ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) Inspection (DAI) on a managed switch compares every ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) reply with the address bindings learned by DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) snooping and drops replies that do not match. A static ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) entry for the gateway on critical machines makes them ignore forged replies for that address. Monitoring tools such as arpwatch, or a simple comparison with the gateway MAC (Media Access Control) recorded in the device registry, reveal the change. Encryption limits the damage: with HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) and the Secure flag, the on-path host sees no cookie. Finally, zoning limits the reach: ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) works only inside one broadcast domain, so an infected workstation in the user zone cannot poison hosts of the server zone behind NM-FW01.


Slide 37DNS cache poisoning and four controls
3.4 Cache protection: the DNS (Domain Name System) cache


A resolver keeps each answer it receives for the duration of its time to live (TTL). In DNS (Domain Name System) cache poisoning, an attacker makes the resolver accept a forged answer, for example a wrong address for the tax website. Every client of that resolver is then sent to the attacker's server until the entry expires; a convincing copy of the login page collects passwords and session cookies. Four controls reduce the risk:


    

  1. DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) validation. Signed zones carry signatures that a validating resolver verifies before caching. Unbound, the resolver used by OPNsense and by the pfSense DNS (Domain Name System) Resolver, supports validation; a validated answer carries the AD (Authenticated Data) flag (https://docs.opnsense.org/manual/unbound.html).
    2. 

  2. Randomisation. Random source ports and random query identifiers make a forged answer much harder to match to a pending query. Keep the resolver updated so these protections stay active.
    3. 

  3. No open resolver. The resolver answers only internal clients, never the Internet.
    4. 

  4. One enforced resolver. Zoning row Z4 lets workstations send DNS (Domain Name System) only to NM-FW01. A firewall rule is what makes that policy real: without it, any program could query an outside resolver the company does not control.
    5. 



Slide 38Web caches and the three caches compared
3.5 Cache protection: web caches


Browsers and shared proxies keep copies of pages to load them faster. For a page that shows client financial records, a stored copy is a disclosure risk on a shared or lost computer, and a stored copy with a session cookie is worse. The response header Cache-Control: no-store forbids any cache from keeping the page (RFC (Request for Comments) 9111: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111). Authenticated pages of NorthMaple's internal service must send it; public pages of the website may be cached normally.


Table 8. Three caches, their poisoning and their protection
CacheWhat it storesHow it is abusedMain protections at NorthMaple
ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) cache (every host)IP (Internet Protocol) address to MAC (Media Access Control) address on the local networkForged ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) replies redirect traffic to an on-path hostDAI (Dynamic ARP Inspection) with DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) snooping; static gateway entry on NM-LWS01; MAC (Media Access Control) baseline in the registry; zoning; HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure)
DNS (Domain Name System) cache (resolver on NM-FW01)Name to IP (Internet Protocol) address, for the TTL (Time To Live) of each recordForged answer sends every client to a lookalike serverDNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) validation; random ports and IDs (Identifiers); no open resolver; rule Z4 enforces one resolver
Web cache (browser, proxy)Copies of pages and resourcesStored authenticated pages disclose client dataCache-Control: no-store on authenticated pages; logout clears the session
Each protection maps to a row of your device registry or of your rule set.


3.6 Tools you can use in the lab


For inspection: the browser's developer tools (Storage or Application tab) show every cookie and its attributes; curl -I or curl -D - prints response headers; ip neigh on Linux and arp -a or Get-NetNeighbor on Windows show the ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) cache; dig +dnssec shows the AD (Authenticated Data) flag. For prevention: switch features (DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) snooping, DAI (Dynamic ARP Inspection), port security), the firewall rules of Lesson 2, and the resolver settings of NM-FW01. Example 3 combines the three inspections in one read-only script.
