Slide 40Example 3: is Marc's session safe?
Real-life example, Lesson 3
Is Marc's session to the internal client portal safe from NM-LWS01's point of view?
Task of this example
From the administrator workstation, run three read-only checks: the ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) cache (gateway MAC (Media Access Control) against the device registry, and duplicate MAC (Media Access Control) addresses), DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) validation by the firewall's resolver, and the cookie and cache headers of the internal HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) service. Produce a PASS, WARN or FAIL line for each control.
How it relates to this lesson
Each check corresponds to one section of the lesson: 3.3 (ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) cache), 3.4 (DNS (Domain Name System) cache) and 3.2 plus 3.5 (Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite, HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) and no-store). The demo data contains one ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) poisoning pattern and one weak cookie, so every kind of result appears.
Where this example and its deliverable return in the scheduled labs
  • LAB_06 part 2 (Class 17): after enabling HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) with a self-signed certificate on an internal service, run the live mode against it and keep the report as validation evidence.
  • LAB_05 device registry (today): the gateway MAC (Media Access Control) baseline used by the script is a column you record in the registry.
  • Final Project Chapter 7: row 6 (a remote worker's traffic intercepted on public Wi-Fi) and row 4 (a worm spreading) are justified with these controls.


Marc reports that the client portal "logged him out and then showed someone else's name" for a second. The IT (Information Technology) administrator suspects either a network problem or an attack and starts with facts that can be collected safely from NM-LWS01, without touching any other system than NorthMaple's own lab machines.


    

  1. Run ./ex3_session_cache_check.sh --demo in class; everyone gets the same sample data and the same results.
    2. 

  2. Pause after the ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) checks: which two findings point to poisoning, and which host is suspect?
    3. 

  3. Pause after the cookie checks: which missing attribute would let the cookie travel in clear text?
    4. 

  4. In your lab, run it without --demo on NM-LWS01 once LAB_06 has an HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) service, and keep ex3_session_cache_report.txt.
    5. 



Deliverable reused later: ex3_session_cache_report.txt from the live run, attached as validation evidence in Chapter 6 (LAB_06) and cited in the Chapter 7 resilience rows.


Code illustration of the real-life example
ex3_session_cache_check.sh
What this code does
The script collects three data sets (ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) cache, DNS (Domain Name System) answer flags, HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) response headers) either from built-in samples (--demo) or from the live system, evaluates eight controls, writes one aligned result line per control to the screen and to a report file, and ends with an overall verdict and an exit code.
How it relates to the lecture
It turns the lesson into observable facts: a changed gateway MAC (Media Access Control) and a duplicate MAC (Media Access Control) are the traces of ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) cache poisoning, the AD (Authenticated Data) flag proves DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) validation, and the Set-Cookie, Strict-Transport-Security and Cache-Control headers show whether a stolen or cached session is possible.
Bashex3_session_cache_check.sh
This player needs JavaScript: open the saved file in a browser. The complete source code is shown below and can be read without it.
Orange line: the line that just ran. The trace was recorded from a real run of this exact file.
Source code: every line of code has its comment above it
1#!/usr/bin/env bash
2# ============================================================================
3# ex3_session_cache_check.sh - Class 12, Lesson 3: Session hijacking prevention and cache protection
4# Cyber Defense 420-D03-AB - Cyber.SoHo - educational use inside an isolated laboratory only.
5#
6# Task: from the administrator workstation NM-LWS01, run three read-only checks that show
7# whether NorthMaple's sessions can be taken over through a poisoned cache or a weak cookie:
8#   1. ARP cache: does the gateway (NM-FW01) still have the MAC address recorded in the
9#      device registry, and does any MAC address claim several IP addresses?
10#   2. DNS cache: does the firewall's resolver validate DNSSEC (the "ad" flag in the answer)?
11#   3. Web session: does the internal HTTPS service mark its session cookie Secure, HttpOnly
12#      and SameSite, send HSTS, and forbid caching of the logged-in page (no-store)?
13# Usage:  ./ex3_session_cache_check.sh --demo   (built-in sample data, works anywhere)
14#         ./ex3_session_cache_check.sh          (live data of NM-LWS01, inside your lab only)
15# Output: a PASS / WARN / FAIL line per control, saved as ex3_session_cache_report.txt, reused
16# in LAB_06 part 2 (HTTPS on an internal service) and in Chapter 7 of the Final Project.
17# Abbreviations: ARP (Address Resolution Protocol), MAC (Media Access Control), IP (Internet
18# Protocol), DNS (Domain Name System), DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions),
19# HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure), HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security),
20# RFC (Request for Comments). The script only reads; it sends nothing but one DNS query and
21# one HTTPS request to your own lab systems.
22# ============================================================================
23 
24# Mode of operation: "--demo" uses the sample data written below; anything else reads the live system.
25MODE="${1:-live}"
26# The gateway of the user zone is the LAN address of NM-FW01.
27GATEWAY_IP="192.168.10.1"
28# The gateway MAC address written in the device registry when NM-FW01 was deployed (Class 11); this is the baseline.
29GATEWAY_MAC_BASELINE="52:54:00:0a:00:01"
30# The DNS resolver of the firewall (Unbound on OPNsense, DNS Resolver on pfSense) that every workstation must use.
31RESOLVER="192.168.10.1"
32# The internal HTTPS service that LAB_06 protects with a self-signed certificate (illustrative address and page).
33SERVICE_URL="https://192.168.30.10/login"
34# The report file that becomes evidence in LAB_06 and in the resilience assessment.
35REPORT="ex3_session_cache_report.txt"
36# Counters of failed controls and of warnings; they decide the final verdict.
37FAILS=0
38# Warnings are weaknesses that do not break the control on their own.
39WARNS=0
40 
41# is_private succeeds only for RFC 1918 addresses, so the live mode can never be pointed at a system outside the lab.
42is_private() {
43  # Regular expression with three alternatives: 10.x.x.x, 172.16.x.x to 172.31.x.x, and 192.168.x.x.
44  [[ "$1" =~ ^(10\.|172\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[01])\.|192\.168\.) ]]
45# The closing brace ends the function.
46}
47 
48# report prints one aligned result line and appends the same line to the report file.
49report() {
50  # printf pads the control name to 38 characters; tee -a shows the line and adds it to the file.
51  printf '%-38s %s\n' "$1" "$2" | tee -a "$REPORT"
52# The closing brace ends the function.
53}
54 
55# demo_arp prints a sample of what "ip neigh show" returns on NM-LWS01 (the kernel's ARP cache).
56demo_arp() {
57  # Sample line 1: the gateway 192.168.10.1 now answers with MAC 52:54:00:66:66:66, not the registry value.
58  printf '%s\n' "192.168.10.1 dev eth0 lladdr 52:54:00:66:66:66 REACHABLE"
59  # Sample line 2: the Windows workstation NM-WS01 with its own MAC address.
60  printf '%s\n' "192.168.10.21 dev eth0 lladdr 52:54:00:0a:00:15 STALE"
61  # Sample line 3: the staff laptop NM-LT01 on the corporate Wi-Fi.
62  printf '%s\n' "192.168.10.50 dev eth0 lladdr 52:54:00:0a:00:32 REACHABLE"
63  # Sample line 4: an unknown machine .77 with the SAME MAC as the "gateway": one device claims two addresses.
64  printf '%s\n' "192.168.10.77 dev eth0 lladdr 52:54:00:66:66:66 REACHABLE"
65# The closing brace ends the function.
66}
67 
68# demo_dig prints the header line that "dig +dnssec" shows when a validating resolver answers.
69demo_dig() {
70  # The flags line: qr = response, rd/ra = recursion desired/available, ad = the resolver validated the DNSSEC signatures.
71  printf '%s\n' ";; flags: qr rd ra ad; QUERY: 1, ANSWER: 2, AUTHORITY: 0, ADDITIONAL: 1"
72# The closing brace ends the function.
73}
74 
75# demo_headers prints the response headers of the internal login page, as "curl -D -" shows them.
76demo_headers() {
77  # Status line: the page was delivered.
78  printf '%s\n' "HTTP/1.1 200 OK"
79  # The session cookie: HttpOnly is present, but Secure and SameSite are missing.
80  printf '%s\n' "Set-Cookie: NMSESSION=4f9c2e7a1b8d; Path=/; HttpOnly"
81  # The page may not be stored by the browser or by any intermediate cache.
82  printf '%s\n' "Cache-Control: no-store"
83  # Content type of the page; no Strict-Transport-Security header follows.
84  printf '%s\n' "Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8"
85# The closing brace ends the function.
86}
87 
88# In live mode, refuse to run if the resolver or the service address is not a private lab address.
89if [[ "$MODE" != "--demo" ]] && { ! is_private "$RESOLVER" || ! is_private "$(cut -d/ -f3 <<< "$SERVICE_URL")"; }; then
90  # Explain why the script stops, then stop with an error code.
91  echo "Refusing to run: targets must be private addresses of your own isolated lab." >&2
92  # Exit code 2 means "configuration refused".
93  exit 2
94# fi ends the if block above.
95fi
96 
97# Temporary files hold the collected data, one file per check.
98ARP_FILE="$(mktemp)"
99# Second temporary file: the DNS answer.
100DIG_FILE="$(mktemp)"
101# Third temporary file: the HTTP response headers.
102HDR_FILE="$(mktemp)"
103# Delete the temporary files whenever the script ends, even after an error.
104trap 'rm -f "$ARP_FILE" "$DIG_FILE" "$HDR_FILE"' EXIT
105# Start a fresh report file with a title line that contains the date and the mode.
106echo "Session and cache protection check - $(date +%F) - mode: $MODE" > "$REPORT"
107 
108# Collect the three data sets: sample data in demo mode...
109if [[ "$MODE" == "--demo" ]]; then
110  # ...the sample ARP cache,
111  demo_arp > "$ARP_FILE"
112  # ...the sample DNS answer,
113  demo_dig > "$DIG_FILE"
114  # ...and the sample response headers.
115  demo_headers > "$HDR_FILE"
116# ...or the live data of NM-LWS01.
117else
118  # The kernel's neighbour table (ARP cache) for IPv4.
119  ip -4 neigh show > "$ARP_FILE"
120  # One DNSSEC-aware query for a signed domain (isc.org) sent to the firewall's resolver only.
121  dig @"$RESOLVER" isc.org +dnssec +noall +comments > "$DIG_FILE"
122  # Response headers only (-D -), body discarded; -k accepts the self-signed LAB_06 certificate, acceptable ONLY for your own lab.
123  curl -sk -D - -o /dev/null "$SERVICE_URL" > "$HDR_FILE"
124# fi ends the if block above.
125fi
126 
127# Check 1a: awk finds the gateway's line and prints the word after "lladdr", which is its MAC address.
128GW_MAC="$(awk -v gw="$GATEWAY_IP" '$1 == gw { for (i = 1; i < NF; i++) if ($i == "lladdr") print $(i + 1) }' "$ARP_FILE")"
129# Compare the current gateway MAC with the registry baseline.
130if [[ "$GW_MAC" == "$GATEWAY_MAC_BASELINE" ]]; then
131  # Same MAC as recorded: the cache entry for the gateway is trustworthy.
132  ARP_GATEWAY="PASS"
133# A different MAC means the entry changed: hardware replacement, or a forged ARP reply.
134else
135  # Mark the control as failed.
136  ARP_GATEWAY="FAIL"
137  # Count the failure.
138  FAILS=$((FAILS + 1))
139# fi ends the if block above.
140fi
141# Write the gateway result with both MAC addresses, so the evidence explains itself.
142report "ARP gateway MAC ($GW_MAC)" "$ARP_GATEWAY (registry: $GATEWAY_MAC_BASELINE)"
143 
144# Check 1b: count how many IP addresses each MAC claims and print the MACs that claim more than one.
145DUP_MACS="$(awk '{ for (i = 1; i < NF; i++) if ($i == "lladdr") n[$(i + 1)]++ } END { for (m in n) if (n[m] > 1) print m }' "$ARP_FILE" | tr '\n' ' ')"
146# An empty list means every MAC answers for one address only.
147if [[ -z "$DUP_MACS" ]]; then
148  # No duplicate: normal situation on a small switched LAN.
149  ARP_DUPLICATES="PASS"
150# A duplicate is a classic sign of ARP cache poisoning (a router with several addresses would be a documented exception).
151else
152  # Mark the control as failed.
153  ARP_DUPLICATES="FAIL"
154  # Count the failure.
155  FAILS=$((FAILS + 1))
156# fi ends the if block above.
157fi
158# Write the duplicate-MAC result.
159report "ARP duplicate MAC addresses" "$ARP_DUPLICATES ${DUP_MACS}"
160 
161# Check 2: keep only the flags line of the DNS answer.
162DNS_FLAGS="$(grep -m1 'flags:' "$DIG_FILE")"
163# The "ad" flag (Authenticated Data) proves the resolver checked the DNSSEC signatures before caching the answer.
164if [[ "$DNS_FLAGS" == *" ad"* ]]; then
165  # Validation is active.
166  DNSSEC="PASS"
167# No "ad" flag: the resolver caches answers it has not verified.
168else
169  # A weakness, reported as a warning.
170  DNSSEC="WARN"
171  # Count the warning.
172  WARNS=$((WARNS + 1))
173# fi ends the if block above.
174fi
175# Write the DNS result.
176report "DNS resolver validates DNSSEC" "$DNSSEC"
177 
178# Check 3: keep the first Set-Cookie header and convert it to lower case for comparisons.
179COOKIE="$(grep -i -m1 '^set-cookie:' "$HDR_FILE" | tr 'A-Z' 'a-z')"
180# Secure: the browser sends the cookie only over HTTPS, never in clear text.
181if [[ "$COOKIE" == *"; secure"* ]]; then C_SECURE="PASS"; else C_SECURE="FAIL"; FAILS=$((FAILS + 1)); fi
182# HttpOnly: scripts running in the page cannot read the cookie, which blocks theft by cross-site scripting.
183if [[ "$COOKIE" == *"; httponly"* ]]; then C_HTTPONLY="PASS"; else C_HTTPONLY="FAIL"; FAILS=$((FAILS + 1)); fi
184# SameSite: the browser does not attach the cookie to requests started by other sites.
185if [[ "$COOKIE" == *"; samesite="* ]]; then C_SAMESITE="PASS"; else C_SAMESITE="WARN"; WARNS=$((WARNS + 1)); fi
186# HSTS: the server orders the browser to use HTTPS only for this site in the future.
187if grep -qi '^strict-transport-security:' "$HDR_FILE"; then HSTS="PASS"; else HSTS="WARN"; WARNS=$((WARNS + 1)); fi
188# no-store: the logged-in page must not be kept in the browser cache or in a shared cache.
189if grep -qi '^cache-control:.*no-store' "$HDR_FILE"; then CACHE="PASS"; else CACHE="WARN"; WARNS=$((WARNS + 1)); fi
190# Write the five web-session results, one line each.
191report "Session cookie flag Secure" "$C_SECURE"
192# HttpOnly result.
193report "Session cookie flag HttpOnly" "$C_HTTPONLY"
194# SameSite result.
195report "Session cookie attribute SameSite" "$C_SAMESITE"
196# HSTS result.
197report "HSTS header present" "$HSTS"
198# Cache-Control result.
199report "Logged-in page not cached (no-store)" "$CACHE"
200 
201# Final verdict: any FAIL means the session can be taken over in at least one documented way.
202if (( FAILS > 0 )); then VERDICT="FAIL"; elif (( WARNS > 0 )); then VERDICT="WARN"; else VERDICT="PASS"; fi
203# Write the summary line with the counts.
204report "Overall ($FAILS fail, $WARNS warn)" "$VERDICT"
205# Exit code 1 lets a scheduler or a later script detect the failure; 0 means every control passed.
206(( FAILS == 0 ))
207

Console output
Step-by-step explanation of ex3_session_cache_check.sh
  1. The first variables hold the mode, the gateway address, the gateway MAC (Media Access Control) recorded in the device registry, the resolver, the internal service URL (Uniform Resource Locator) and the report file name. FAILS and WARNS count the results.
  2. is_private accepts only RFC (Request for Comments) 1918 addresses. In live mode, the script refuses to run if the resolver or the service is outside the private ranges, so it cannot be pointed at a system outside the lab.
  3. report prints one aligned line and appends it to the report file with tee -a, so screen and evidence always match.
  4. demo_arp, demo_dig and demo_headers print sample data. The ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) sample shows the gateway with an unexpected MAC (Media Access Control) that also answers for .77; the headers lack Secure, SameSite and HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security).
  5. mktemp creates three temporary files and trap deletes them when the script ends, even after an error.
  6. In demo mode the samples are written to the files; in live mode, ip -4 neigh show, dig +dnssec and curl -D - collect the same information from NM-LWS01.
  7. awk extracts the gateway's MAC (Media Access Control); comparing it with the baseline gives FAIL in the demo (52:54:00:66:66:66 instead of 52:54:00:0a:00:01).
  8. A second awk counts how many IP (Internet Protocol) addresses each MAC (Media Access Control) claims; 52:54:00:66:66:66 claims two, which is the classic poisoning pattern: FAIL.
  9. grep keeps the flags line of the DNS (Domain Name System) answer; the presence of " ad" means the resolver validated the signatures: PASS.
  10. The Set-Cookie header is converted to lower case and tested for secure, httponly and samesite; then grep looks for Strict-Transport-Security and Cache-Control: no-store.
  11. The overall verdict is FAIL when any control failed, WARN when only warnings exist, PASS otherwise. The demo ends with 3 fail, 2 warn: FAIL, and exit code 1.

Question 1 of 6. Multiple choice, one answer.
The internal portal sends: Set-Cookie: NMSESSION=4f9c...; Path=/; HttpOnly. Which risk remains open?
Show hint
Which attribute controls the channel over which the cookie may travel?
Show answer and explanations
Correct answer: d
  • a) Incorrect. HttpOnly is present in this header.
  • b) Incorrect. No attribute here causes deletion; Path=/ only defines where it is sent.
  • c) Incorrect. SameSite limits cross-site sending; its absence does not disable the cookie.
  • d) Correct. Without Secure, any HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) request to the site carries the cookie in clear text.
Question 2 of 6. Multiple choice, one answer.
On NM-WS01, the ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) cache shows the MAC (Media Access Control) 52:54:00:66:66:66 for both 192.168.10.1 (the gateway) and 192.168.10.77. What is the most likely explanation?
Show hint
One device claims to be two addresses, one of which is the gateway.
Show answer and explanations
Correct answer: b
  • a) Incorrect. DNS (Domain Name System) maps names to IP (Internet Protocol) addresses; this table maps IP (Internet Protocol) addresses to MAC (Media Access Control) addresses.
  • b) Correct. A changed gateway MAC (Media Access Control) shared with another host is the classic poisoning pattern.
  • c) Incorrect. The firewall's state table has no effect on hosts' ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) caches.
  • d) Incorrect. Fixation concerns session identifiers, not link-layer addresses.
Question 3 of 6. Multiple choice, one answer.
Why does zoning row Z4 (workstations send DNS (Domain Name System) only to NM-FW01) help against DNS (Domain Name System) cache poisoning?
Show hint
Which resolvers can the company actually protect and monitor?
Show answer and explanations
Correct answer: c
  • a) Incorrect. A firewall rule filters traffic; it does not encrypt it.
  • b) Incorrect. Expiry depends on the TTL (Time To Live) of each record, not on firewall rules.
  • c) Correct. The rule turns the resolver policy into something the network enforces.
  • d) Incorrect. Z4 allows DNS (Domain Name System) to the firewall's resolver; blocking all DNS (Domain Name System) would break name resolution.
Question 4 of 6. Multiple choice, one answer.
Which measure specifically defeats session fixation?
Show hint
In fixation, the attacker already knows the identifier the victim will use.
Show answer and explanations
Correct answer: a
  • a) Correct. The identifier known to the attacker becomes worthless at authentication.
  • b) Incorrect. no-store protects cached copies of pages, not identifiers.
  • c) Incorrect. DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) protects name resolution, not session management.
  • d) Incorrect. ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) filtering has no relation to how a web application assigns identifiers.
Question 5 of 6. Multiple select, several answers.
Which controls reduce the risk that a NorthMaple session cookie is stolen or reused? (Select 4)
Show hint
Choose controls on the channel, on the cookie itself, and on the session lifetime.
Show answer and explanations
Correct answer: a, d, e, f
  • a) Correct. A stolen identifier stops working quickly.
  • b) Incorrect. IDs (Identifiers) in URLs leak through logs, history and shared links.
  • c) Incorrect. Cached authenticated pages disclose data; they need no-store.
  • d) Correct. The cookie is not attached to requests from other sites.
  • e) Correct. They block clear-text transport and script access.
  • f) Correct. The cookie never travels unencrypted.
Question 6 of 6. Multiple select, several answers.
Which statements about ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) and DNS (Domain Name System) cache protection are correct? (Select 3)
Show hint
One statement for each cache, plus one about the reach of ARP (Address Resolution Protocol).
Show answer and explanations
Correct answer: b, c, e
  • a) Incorrect. An open resolver is abused for poisoning attempts and for amplification.
  • b) Correct. It is the switch-level defense.
  • c) Correct. A router or firewall between zones stops ARP (Address Resolution Protocol).
  • d) Incorrect. Static entries are set on the machines you protect, such as NM-LWS01.
  • e) Correct. Unvalidated forgeries are rejected.
  • f) Incorrect. ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) has no authentication at all; that is why poisoning works.
Lesson 4 of 4, about 11 minutes
DoS (Denial-of-Service) attack defense strategies: basic, practical measures
Slide 41DoS attack defense strategies: basic, practical measures
Terms to learn in this lesson
Availability
The property that a service works for its authorised users when they need it; the A of the CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability) triad.
DoS (Denial-of-Service)
An attack that makes a service unavailable by exhausting one of its resources or by triggering a fault.
DDoS (Distributed Denial-of-Service)
A DoS (Denial-of-Service) attack sent from many sources at once, often a botnet of compromised machines (see the malware families of Class 4).
Volumetric attack
Fills the network link with more traffic than it can carry; measured in bits per second.
Protocol (state-exhaustion) attack
Fills tables that track connections, such as a firewall's state table or a server's half-open connection queue; measured in packets per second.
Application-layer attack
Sends valid-looking requests that exhaust the service itself (HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) floods, very slow requests); measured in requests per second.
SYN (Synchronize) flood
Many TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) SYN (Synchronize) packets, often with forged sources, that leave half-open connections waiting for an ACK (Acknowledgment) that never comes.
SYN (Synchronize) cookies
A TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) technique (RFC (Request for Comments) 4987) in which the server encodes the connection data in its sequence number and allocates memory only when the final ACK (Acknowledgment) returns.
Reflection and amplification
The attacker sends small requests with the victim's forged address to public servers, which send much larger answers to the victim.
Ingress filtering (BCP (Best Current Practice) 38)
Dropping packets whose source address cannot be legitimate on that interface, which stops address spoofing at the network edge.


Confidentiality and integrity have been the focus of the previous lessons. A denial-of-service attack targets the third property, availability: the attacker does not need to read or change anything, only to make the service stop working for the people who need it (CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) overview: https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/news/understanding-denial-service-attacks). For NorthMaple, whose clients upload documents in tax season, one day without the public website is a real business loss.


Slide 42Three classes of DoS attack
4.1 Classify the attack by the resource it exhausts


Every service depends on finite resources: the capacity of the network link, the tables that track connections, and the processor, memory and worker processes of the server. A DoS (Denial-of-Service) attack exhausts one of them, and the class of the attack determines where it can be stopped (Figure 8, after the example).


Table 9. The three classes of denial-of-service attack
ClassResource exhaustedUnit that growsTypical exampleLayer that can absorb it
VolumetricCapacity of the WAN (Wide Area Network) linkBits per secondUDP (User Datagram Protocol) reflection and amplification (DNS (Domain Name System), NTP (Network Time Protocol))Upstream: provider, mitigation service, CDN (Content Delivery Network)
Protocol / state exhaustionState table of the firewall; half-open queue of the serverPackets per secondSYN (Synchronize) floodNM-FW01 and the server's TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) stack
Application layerProcessor, memory, worker processes of the serviceRequests per secondHTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) flood; very slow requestsNM-WEB01 (and a CDN (Content Delivery Network) in front of it)
Distributed (DDoS (Distributed Denial-of-Service)) describes the number of sources, not the class: each class can be distributed.


Slide 43Where each class hits the network
A volumetric attack fills the link. If NorthMaple's connection carries a known number of bits per second, any flood larger than that saturates it before a single packet reaches NM-FW01. No setting on the firewall can help, because the congestion happens upstream; only the Internet service provider or a mitigation service can filter that traffic before it enters the link. Many volumetric attacks use reflection and amplification: the attacker sends small queries with the victim's forged source address to open DNS (Domain Name System) resolvers, NTP (Network Time Protocol) servers or similar services, which return answers many times larger to the victim.


A protocol attack fills tables. In a SYN (Synchronize) flood, the attacker sends many SYN (Synchronize) packets, often with forged sources. The server answers each with SYN-ACK (Synchronize-Acknowledgment) and keeps a half-open entry while waiting for the final ACK (Acknowledgment), which never comes. When the queue is full, real clients are refused. A stateful firewall has the same weakness: each new connection consumes an entry in its state table.


An application-layer attack sends requests that look legitimate: thousands of searches or page loads per second, or connections that send headers extremely slowly so that each one occupies a worker process for minutes. The traffic volume may be small, which makes these attacks hard to separate from real users.


Slide 44Practical measures for a small company (1/2)
4.2 Practical measures for a small company


    

  1. Know your baseline. Record normal values for bandwidth, packets per second, states in the firewall table and requests per second on NM-WEB01. Without a baseline, nobody can tell an attack from a busy Monday.
    2. 

  2. Keep the attack surface small. Zoning row Z1 publishes one service, HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) on NM-WEB01. Every service that is not published cannot be flooded directly.
    3. 

  3. Slide 45Limit states per source on the publishing rule
    Limit states on the publishing rule. pfSense and OPNsense let a pass rule cap the total number of states it may create, the number of states per source and the rate of new connections per source (Figure 9, after the example). A single abusive source then stops receiving new states while other visitors continue. Choose the limits from your baseline, and check the exact option names in your appliance version.
    4. 

  4. Protect the TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) handshake. SYN (Synchronize) cookies on the web server, or a SYN (Synchronize) proxy on the firewall where the appliance offers one, stop half-open connections from consuming memory (RFC (Request for Comments) 4987: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4987). Shorter timeouts for half-open states have the same aim.
    5. 

  5. Slide 46Practical measures for a small company (2/2)
    Filter spoofed addresses in both directions. On WAN (Wide Area Network), the options that block private and bogon source networks drop packets whose source cannot be real on the Internet. On the internal interfaces, rules that allow only the zone's own network as source (LAN_NET, DMZ_NET) stop NorthMaple's machines from sending forged packets. This is ingress filtering, described in BCP (Best Current Practice) 38 (RFC (Request for Comments) 2827: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2827).
    6. 

  6. Do not become a reflector. The firewall's resolver answers only internal clients; no internal service is published without a zoning row.
    7. 

  7. Protect the service itself. Rate limits per client and timeouts for slow clients on the web server; static or cached pages where possible; hosting the public website with a provider or content delivery network (CDN) that absorbs floods.
    8. 

  8. Prepare the upstream contact. Write down, before any incident, how to reach the ISP (Internet Service Provider)'s support for DDoS (Distributed Denial-of-Service), which mitigation the contract includes, and who inside NorthMaple may decide to take the website offline.
    9. 



Table 10. Practical DoS (Denial-of-Service) measures by layer
LayerMeasurePrepared whenWhere it is documented
UpstreamProvider DDoS (Distributed Denial-of-Service) contact, mitigation terms, optional CDN (Content Delivery Network) for the websiteBefore any incidentDevice registry (WAN (Wide Area Network) link entry); incident plan
NM-FW01State limit, per-source state limit, new-connection rate per source on rule Z1LAB_05 part 2Rule set, advanced-options column
NM-FW01Block private and bogon sources on WAN (Wide Area Network); source = own network on internal interfacesLAB_05 part 2Rule set and interface settings
NM-FW01SYN (Synchronize) proxy or shorter half-open timeouts where availableLAB_05 part 2 (optional)Rule set notes (check your appliance version)
NM-WEB01SYN (Synchronize) cookies, request rate limits, timeouts for slow clients, cachingHost hardening (LAB_03 review)Chapter 3 notes
MonitoringBaseline of bandwidth, states and requests per second; IDS (Intrusion Detection System) alertsLAB_04 and LAB_05Chapters 4 and 5
OrganisationWho decides, who communicates, timeline templateBefore any incidentChapter 7, resilience row 7
Option names differ between pfSense and OPNsense versions; confirm them in your appliance before documenting.


Slide 47DoS triage: six stages, explained in theory
4.3 Theoretical explanation: the most common DoS (Denial-of-Service) triage sequence


By course decision, no DoS (Denial-of-Service) triage script is provided in this module. The procedure is explained theoretically, in the form most incident response teams apply it.


Triage means deciding quickly what is happening and what to do first. The six stages below are applied in order, and the last stage prepares the next incident (Figure 7; use the stage buttons to walk through it).


    

  1. Detect and confirm. An alert (monitoring, IDS (Intrusion Detection System), user complaints) reports slowness or failure. Compare current measurements with the baseline. A marketing campaign, a failed disk or an expired certificate can look like an attack; confirm before acting.
    2. 

  2. Scope and classify. Identify which service is affected, which resource is exhausted (link, state table, server), whether the unit that grows is bits, packets or requests per second, and whether the traffic comes from one source or from many. This places the attack in one of the three classes of section 4.1.
    3. 

  3. Contain at the right layer. Volumetric: contact the provider or activate the mitigation service; local changes cannot help. Protocol: state and rate limits, SYN (Synchronize) cookies or SYN (Synchronize) proxy, temporary blocks of the worst sources if they are few. Application: request rate limits, caching, blocking the request pattern, scaling the service.
    4. 

  4. Communicate and escalate. Inform management, the provider and, if clients are affected, the clients, following the incident plan. Keep a timeline with times, measurements and decisions.
    5. 

  5. Monitor and adjust. Verify that each measure helps legitimate users and does not block them. Attackers change technique; adjust the limits step by step.
    6. 

  6. Recover and document. Remove temporary measures in a controlled way, restore normal service, and record what happened, what worked and what will change: new limits in the rule set, new registry entries, updated contacts. This record is the justification of a resilience row.
    7.

Slide 49Example 4: the website stops answering at 9:05
Real-life example, Lesson 4
Tax season, 9:05: NorthMaple's website stops answering
Task of this example
Use the symptoms of a fictional incident to classify the attack, decide which defense layer must respond, and draft row 7 of the resilience assessment ("A DoS (Denial-of-Service) attempt targets the public service") in your own words.
How it relates to this lesson
The example applies section 4.1 (classification by exhausted resource), section 4.2 (practical measures by layer) and section 4.3 (the triage stages), without any script.
Where this example and its deliverable return in the scheduled labs
  • LAB_05 part 2 (today): record the state and connection limits you set on the WAN (Wide Area Network) publishing rule (Z1) in the advanced-options column of your rule set.
  • Final Project Chapter 7 (Classes 18-19): this analysis becomes row 7 of the resilience assessment, with your verdict and your one-sentence justification.
  • LAB_05 device registry: add the provider's DDoS (Distributed Denial-of-Service) contact and the mitigation terms as a note on the WAN (Wide Area Network) link entry.


This scenario happens only inside the fictional company. At 9:05, clients call: the upload page of the NorthMaple website does not load. Staff can still open the file server, but their web browsing is slow. The firewall dashboard of NM-FW01 shows the state table at 97 percent of its maximum, almost all entries half-open connections toward NM-WEB01:443, coming from several thousand different source addresses. The WAN (Wide Area Network) link is at 40 percent of its capacity. The web server's processor is almost idle.


    

  1. Classify. Which resource is exhausted: the link, the state table, or the server? What does the idle processor tell you?
    2. 

  2. Locate the defense. Using Figure 7, which layer can absorb this class, and which layer would be needed if the link were at 100 percent instead?
    3. 

  3. Choose measures. From Table 10, list the measures that apply now and the ones you should have prepared before.
    4. 

  4. Draft row 7. Write the defense layers (Chapters 1 to 6), your verdict (Withstands, Partly, Does not) and one sentence of justification that names your own configuration.
    5. 



Deliverable reused later: the draft of resilience row 7 and the list of limits configured on rule Z1. Both are completed in Chapter 7 of the Final Project at Classes 18 and 19; the verdict must match what your laboratory configuration really does.

Four multiple-choice and two multiple-select questions
Question 1 of 6. Multiple choice, one answer.
NM-FW01's state table is almost full of half-open connections to NM-WEB01:443 from thousands of sources; the WAN (Wide Area Network) link is at 40 percent. Which class of attack is this?
Show hint
Which resource is exhausted, and which one is not?
Show answer and explanations
Correct answer: a
  • a) Correct. Half-open entries fill the table while the link still has capacity.
  • b) Incorrect. Many sources make it distributed; the link at 40 percent shows it is not volumetric.
  • c) Incorrect. Half-open connections never reach the application; no request is sent.
  • d) Incorrect. ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) poisoning redirects traffic inside one LAN (Local Area Network); it does not create Internet connections.
Question 2 of 6. Multiple choice, one answer.
The WAN (Wide Area Network) link of NorthMaple is saturated at 100 percent by UDP (User Datagram Protocol) traffic from thousands of DNS (Domain Name System) servers. Which response can work?
Show hint
Where is the congestion located?
Show answer and explanations
Correct answer: c
  • a) Incorrect. The rule drops packets after they have already crossed the saturated link.
  • b) Incorrect. State limits act on the firewall, not on link capacity, and this traffic creates no states.
  • c) Correct. The link is full before NM-FW01 sees anything; filtering must happen before the link.
  • d) Incorrect. The server is not the exhausted resource.
Question 3 of 6. Multiple choice, one answer.
What does a per-source state limit on the WAN (Wide Area Network) publishing rule (Z1) achieve?
Show hint
Think of one abusive address among many normal visitors.
Show answer and explanations
Correct answer: b
  • a) Incorrect. Limits count connections; encryption is TLS (Transport Layer Security)'s job.
  • b) Correct. The limit isolates the abusive source without closing the service for everyone.
  • c) Incorrect. Thousands of sources each below the limit still exhaust resources, and volumetric floods never reach the rule.
  • d) Incorrect. The limit applies per source, not to the whole interface.
Question 4 of 6. Multiple choice, one answer.
Why does NorthMaple keep its firewall resolver closed to Internet clients?
Show hint
What can an attacker do with a resolver that answers anyone?
Show answer and explanations
Correct answer: d
  • a) Incorrect. DNS (Domain Name System) works over any interface; the restriction is a security choice.
  • b) Incorrect. Validation and access control are independent settings.
  • c) Incorrect. The resolver's exposure does not affect website speed for visitors.
  • d) Correct. Open resolvers answer forged queries with large responses sent to the victim.
Question 5 of 6. Multiple select, several answers.
Which are basic, practical DoS (Denial-of-Service) measures for a small company such as NorthMaple? (Select 4)
Show hint
Measures at the firewall, at the server, upstream, and in preparation.
Show answer and explanations
Correct answer: a, b, e, f
  • a) Correct. It isolates abusive sources at the firewall.
  • b) Correct. It protects the handshake from half-open floods.
  • c) Incorrect. An open resolver becomes an amplification tool.
  • d) Incorrect. Every published service increases the attack surface.
  • e) Correct. It is needed to detect and confirm an attack.
  • f) Correct. Volumetric floods need the upstream layer.
Question 6 of 6. Multiple select, several answers.
Which statements about the DoS (Denial-of-Service) triage sequence are correct? (Select 3)
Show hint
Order of the stages, and what each one produces.
Show answer and explanations
Correct answer: a, b, c
  • a) Correct. Documentation prepares the next incident.
  • b) Correct. A surge or a fault must be excluded first.
  • c) Correct. Upstream, firewall or server depends on the class.
  • d) Incorrect. Stakeholders must be informed according to the incident plan, whatever the duration.
  • e) Incorrect. Shutting down the service completes the attacker's goal; it is a last resort decided by management.
  • f) Incorrect. Triage is a decision procedure; tools help but do not replace it.

LAB_05 part 2 in summary: what you build after the break
Slide 50LAB_05 part 2: what you build after the break


This is a summary only. The complete step-by-step LAB_05 brief is published separately and is the document of record for steps, addressing and due date.


Where LAB_05 stands


Part 1 (Class 11) deployed NM-FW01 as a pfSense or OPNsense virtual machine in front of the company network, secured its management access (strong credentials, HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) management, SSH (Secure Shell) only where needed, management limited to NM-LWS01) and started the company device registry.


What part 2 asks you to do (Class 12)


    

  1. Create the firewall rules that enforce your Class 2 zoning table, on the ingress interface of each flow, in an order that avoids shadowing, with the zoning row identifier in every description (Lesson 2).
    2. 

  2. Replace the installation's broad LAN (Local Area Network) rule with your specific rules, keeping management from NM-LWS01 working at every step.
    3. 

  3. Validate every rule with simple allowed and blocked connection tests, from a machine in the source zone, and capture the firewall log line of each block.
    4. 

  4. Complete the device registry: every network device and appliance with its role, model or virtual machine, software version, management access method and update status.
    5. 



Deliverables


The firewall rule set (export or table), the device registry, and the validation evidence. Together they form the network-security chapter: Chapter 5 of the Final Project and Chapter 5 of the Course Procedure Manual, written with the standard template (objective, environment, numbered procedure, validation, problems and fixes, AI (Artificial Intelligence) disclosure). LAB_05 carries 5 percent of the course grade; Chapter 5 of the Final Project is graded 1.0 point for "exists and works", 0.5 for "validated" and 0.5 for "justified".


Examples 1 and 2 of today give you the reasoning and the skeleton of the rule set and the test plan. Use your own zoning table and your own addresses. If you use an AI (Artificial Intelligence) tool while documenting, disclose the model and the exact prompts in section 5.6 of the chapter. The model drafts. The analyst decides. The analyst's name goes on the record.

Educational purpose and acceptable use


The Material shows how to protect systems, not how to attack the systems of others. Practise only inside your personal, isolated laboratory environment, or on systems for which you hold explicit written permission obtained before you start. Never scan, probe, attack, intercept, monitor or access any system, network, wireless network or account that is not yours. All test traffic of this class, including every connection test of LAB_05 and every run of the example scripts, is generated inside your own laboratory, against your own virtual machines only.


Legal warning


Unauthorized computer access or use is a criminal offence. In Canada, the Criminal Code contains, among other provisions, section 342.1 (unauthorized use of a computer), section 342.2 (possession of a device to obtain unauthorized use of a computer) and section 430(1.1) (mischief in relation to computer data); penalties can include imprisonment. Personal information in your laboratory records is subject to Quebec's private-sector privacy law as amended by Law 25 and to PIPEDA (Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act); keep real personal data out of your deliverables. Outside Canada, comparable laws apply, for example the GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) in the European Union, the US (United States) CFAA (Computer Fraud and Abuse Act) (18 U.S.C. (United States Code) §1030), EU (European Union) Directive 2013/40/EU (European Union) and the Spanish Ley Orgánica 10/1995 (Código Penal). If you are located elsewhere, the laws of your own jurisdiction apply. The policies of your college apply in addition to the law. If an activity seems to touch a system you do not own, stop and ask the instructor.
